quote: which may or may not happen to be shared by any other philosopher’s view of reflection
content: The view is shared, and it has a literature. Braithwaite (Scientific Explanation, 1953; book, no DOI) and Black (1958) held that induction can be supported by inductive arguments without vicious circularity, because the circle runs through a rule of inference rather than through a premise. Van Cleve (1984) defended the idea against Salmon (1957)'s counter-inductive objection. Bartley's pan-critical rationalism, which the commenter raised, has its own well-known problems of self-reference. The essay announces its distinguishing features without checking whether they distinguish it from anything. So it never meets the objection that has dogged this exact position for seventy years: every method, including crazy ones, can support itself in the same way.

quote: I strongly suspect that a correctly built AI, in pondering modifications to the part of its source code that implements Occamian reasoning, will not have to do anything special as it ponders
content: The author's own research program later found that it does have to do something special. MIRI tried to formalize an agent that trusts a successor built on its own reasoning, and ran into Löb's theorem. A consistent system cannot prove that its own proofs are sound, so a naive agent can't vouch for its successor (Yudkowsky & Herreshoff, "Tiling Agents for Self-Modifying AI, and the Löbian Obstacle," MIRI technical report, 2013; no DOI). Demski & Garrabrant (2019) catalogue the broader problems of "embedded agency." The people best placed to test this suspicion tested it, and it failed. The essay treats reflection as "nothing special"; MIRI spent a decade trying to rescue that idea.

quote: we’ve concluded that differential equations (which few humans master) are actually simpler (in an information-theoretic sense) than heroic mythology
content: Nobody has concluded this in the information-theoretic sense, because nobody can compute it. Description length depends on the choice of reference machine, and the invariance theorem guarantees agreement between machines only up to a constant that can be arbitrarily large. Relative to a language in which "an angry god did it" is a primitive, Thor is shorter. Maxwell's equations are simpler than Thor in the sense that matters: they compress vast amounts of data about lightning that Thor does not. But that is a claim about compressing observations, not about the complexity of the two hypotheses taken in the abstract. The gap between the two is exactly the problem of priors that the sequence treats as solved.

quote: by appealing to E. T. Jaynes’s principle that we should always use all the information available to us
content: This is an equivocation. Jaynes's principle, like Carnap's requirement of total evidence, says to condition on all relevant data. It says nothing about which rules of inference to adopt. Using induction to evaluate induction adds no information, since the data are the same whether or not you reason about them in a circle. The principle licenses conditioning on induction's track record. It doesn't license treating that record as non-circular support for induction, which is the question at issue.

quote: But I haven’t yet sat down and formalized the exact difference—my reflective theory is something I’m trying to work out, not something I have in hand.
content: This admission deserves more weight than the essay gives it. The object-level/meta-level distinction is what separates the book's justification of induction, Occam's razor and morality from the circular reasoning it condemns in believers. "Changing Your Metaethics" cites this essay as having explained the difference, but by the author's own account the explanation doesn't exist yet. A distinction that can't be stated can't be applied. And when only its author applies it, it will tend to sort his own loops as reflective and everyone else's as circular.

quote: If you wouldn’t want the AI to rewrite its source code to not use induction, your philosophy had better not label induction as unjustifiable.
content: This conflates keeping a tool with justifying it. Hume held both that induction can't be rationally justified and that we can't and shouldn't stop using it, and there is no inconsistency. "Unjustifiable" is a claim about the grounds of a belief, not advice to abandon it. An AI designer's reluctance to delete induction shows that induction is indispensable, which no skeptic denies. It doesn't supply the justification the skeptic says is missing.
